### Problem: Merge Sorted Array {#sec-tp-p3-a}

::: {.p-statement}
Two sorted arrays. $\mathit{nums1}$ has length $m + n$ with its first $m$ entries valid and the last $n$ set to $0$ (scratch space); $\mathit{nums2}$ has length $n$. $0 \le m, n \le 200$, $1 \le m + n \le 200$, $-10^9 \le$ values $\le 10^9$. Merge $\mathit{nums2}$ into $\mathit{nums1}$ **in place** so that $\mathit{nums1}$ holds all $m + n$ values sorted. No return value — you mutate $\mathit{nums1}$.

Source: [LC 88 · Merge Sorted Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-sorted-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Merging two sorted runs from the *front* needs a separate output buffer, because writing the smallest value into $\mathit{nums1}[0]$ would clobber a value you have not read yet. But $\mathit{nums1}$'s tail is free space, and both inputs are sorted — so fill **from the back**: the largest of the remaining values always belongs at the current far-right slot, and that slot is one you have already vacated or that was free from the start.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Merge into a copy (front).** Take $\mathit{nums1}[:m] + \mathit{nums2}$, sort, copy back. $O((m+n)\log(m+n))$ — the definition with an ordering hammer attached; baseline and oracle.
2. **Two-way merge into a fresh buffer.** The textbook $\text{std::merge}$ walk: two front pointers, always copy the smaller head into the next output slot. $O(m+n)$ time — optimal speed, but it still pays $O(m+n)$ extra space, which the problem's framing (the zeros *are* your buffer) is nudging you to avoid.
3. **Fill from the back.** Three pointers: $i = m-1$, $j = n-1$, write position $p = m+n-1$; drop the larger of $\mathit{nums1}[i], \mathit{nums2}[j]$ into slot $p$ and step left. Stop when $\mathit{nums2}$ is exhausted; whatever is left in $\mathit{nums1}$'s head is already in place. $O(m+n)$, $O(1)$ space.

**Invariant.** Slots $p+1 \dots m+n-1$ already hold the largest $m+n-1-p$ values in sorted order, and $i, j$ point at the largest not-yet-placed values of the two runs — so the back never holds a value still needing to be read. In the fresh-buffer version the dual invariant is "out[:k] holds the k smallest values in order, and both heads are larger than everything written" — same merge skeleton, different direction.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Merge into a copy

::: {.form-next}
Read the valid head of $\mathit{nums1}$, append $\mathit{nums2}$, sort, and write the result back. Two lines and obviously right — the cost is the $O(m+n)$ auxiliary array *and* an $O(\log)$ factor you did not need, because both halves were already ordered. Baseline for the stress check, and worth stating precisely: correctness is trivial here, which is what makes it a fair oracle.

**"Merge", in plain words.** To *merge* two sorted lists means to weave them into one sorted list. The lazy way here is to throw everything together and re-sort it with an ordering hammer — correct, but it ignores that the two halves are *already* sorted.

**Worked example.** $\mathit{nums1} = [1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0]$ with $m = 3$ (so the valid head is $[1, 2, 3]$ and the three zeros are scratch), $\mathit{nums2} = [2, 5, 6]$ with $n = 3$. Head $+$ nums2 $= [1, 2, 3, 2, 5, 6]$, sorted $= [1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]$, written back into $\mathit{nums1}$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def merge_copy(nums1, m, nums2, n):
    a = nums1[:m] + nums2
    a.sort()
    nums1[:m + n] = a
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - copy-based baseline
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
void mergeCopy(vector<int>& n1, int m, vector<int>& n2, int n) {
    vector<int> head(n1.begin(), n1.begin() + m);
    merge(head.begin(), head.end(), n2.begin(), n2.end(), n1.begin());
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `nums1[:m]` slices off only the *valid* leading entries (the trailing zeros are scratch and must be ignored), and `+ nums2` glues the second run on the end. `a.sort()` re-orders the combined list — the wasteful step, since it redoes work the sortedness already gave us. `nums1[:m + n] = a` writes the result back into $\mathit{nums1}$'s own slots (a slice assignment, so the caller's array is mutated in place, as required). Clear and correct; the $O(m+n)$ buffer `a` and the $O((m+n)\log)$ sort are what the next two rungs claw back.

#### Two-way merge into a fresh buffer

::: {.form-next}
Drop the sort but keep the buffer: two pointers read each run's smallest remaining head, and the smaller head is appended to a fresh output — the merge step of merge sort, written front-to-back exactly as @sec-tp-merge's skeleton demands. $O(m+n)$ time matches the back-fill, but the extra array is what the problem forbids, so this rung exists to *name the trade*: same speed, worse space, and a final copy-back over the top of $\mathit{nums1}$.

**The two-pointer merge, in plain words.** Both runs are sorted, so their *smallest* remaining value is always at one of the two front heads. Compare the two heads, copy the smaller into the next output slot, and advance that head. Repeating merges in linear time without ever re-sorting — this is exactly the merge step you will meet again inside merge sort.

**Worked example.** head $= [1, 2, 3]$, $\mathit{nums2} = [2, 5, 6]$. Heads $1$ vs $2$ → take $1$. $2$ vs $2$ → take nums1's $2$ (the $\le$ tie-break). $3$ vs $2$ → take $2$. $3$ vs $5$ → take $3$. nums1 head is spent, so append the rest $5, 6$: out $= [1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("merge", "front")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def merge_front(nums1, m, nums2, n):
    out = []
    i, j = 0, 0                       # heads of the two runs
    while i < m or j < n:
        if j >= n or (i < m and nums1[i] <= nums2[j]):
            out.append(nums1[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(nums2[j]); j += 1
    nums1[:m + n] = out

for _ in range(400):
    a = sorted(random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 6)))
    b = sorted(random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 6)))
    buf = a + [0] * len(b)
    merge_front(buf, len(a), b, len(b))
    assert buf == sorted(a + b)
n5 = [1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0]; merge_front(n5, 3, [2, 5, 6], 3)
assert n5 == [1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]                        # the board sample
print("merge_front OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - textbook front merge into a fresh buffer
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
void mergeFront(vector<int>& n1, int m, vector<int>& n2, int n) {
    vector<int> out; out.reserve(m + n);
    int i = 0, j = 0;
    while (i < m || j < n) {
        if (j >= n || (i < m && n1[i] <= n2[j])) out.push_back(n1[i++]);
        else                                     out.push_back(n2[j++]);
    }
    copy(out.begin(), out.end(), n1.begin());
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `i, j = 0, 0` are the two read heads. The loop `while i < m or j < n` runs until *both* runs are drained. The test `if j >= n or (i < m and nums1[i] <= nums2[j])` means "take from nums1 if nums2 is already empty (`j >= n`) or else nums1's head is no bigger than nums2's"; the `<=` is what keeps the merge *stable* (equal values keep their source order). Whichever branch fires, we `append` that head and step only that pointer. `nums1[:m + n] = out` copies the finished buffer back in place — the extra array is the one thing the problem asked us to avoid.

#### Fill from the back

::: {.form-next}
The in-place merge the problem is really about. Because the free space is at the *tail* and the largest remaining value always goes to the *tail*, the write pointer never lands on data still to be read — the reason the front-fill would corrupt the array simply does not apply going backwards. Stop as soon as $\mathit{nums2}$ runs out; the leftover prefix of $\mathit{nums1}$ is already correct.

**Worked example.** $\mathit{nums1} = [1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0]$, $\mathit{nums2} = [2, 5, 6]$. Start $i=2$ (val $3$), $j=2$ (val $6$), write $p=5$. $3>6$? no → write $6$ at slot $5$, $j\to1, p\to4$. $3>5$? no → write $5$ at $4$, $j\to0, p\to3$. $3>2$? yes → write $3$ at $3$, $i\to1, p\to2$. $2>2$? no → write $2$ at $2$, $j\to-1$ **stop**. Slots $0,1$ still hold $[1, 2]$ — already correct — giving $[1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("merge", "back")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-merge-sorted-back
def merge(nums1, m, nums2, n):        # fill from the back
    i, j, p = m - 1, n - 1, m + n - 1
    while j >= 0:                     # nums2 is the only one that can clobber
        if i >= 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j]:
            nums1[p] = nums1[i]; i -= 1
        else:
            nums1[p] = nums2[j]; j -= 1
        p -= 1

n1 = [1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0]; merge(n1, 3, [2, 5, 6], 3)
assert n1 == [1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]                                   # the board sample
n2 = [0]; merge(n2, 0, [1], 1); assert n2 == [1]
n3 = [1]; merge(n3, 1, [], 0); assert n3 == [1]
n4 = [2, 0]; merge(n4, 1, [1], 1); assert n4 == [1, 2]
for _ in range(400):
    a = sorted(random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 6)))
    b = sorted(random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 6)))
    buf = a + [0] * len(b)
    merge(buf, len(a), b, len(b))
    assert buf == sorted(a + b)
print("merge OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void merge(vector<int>& nums1, int m, vector<int>& nums2, int n) {
    int i = m - 1, j = n - 1, p = m + n - 1;
    while (j >= 0) {
        if (i >= 0 && nums1[i] > nums2[j]) nums1[p--] = nums1[i--];
        else                               nums1[p--] = nums2[j--];
    }
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `i, j, p = m - 1, n - 1, m + n - 1` start at the last valid nums1 value, the last nums2 value, and the very last slot. `while j >= 0` drains $\mathit{nums2}$ — the only run whose leftovers would *not* already be in place. `if i >= 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j]` writes the larger of the two back-tails into slot $p$ and steps that run's pointer left (`i -= 1`); the `else` covers both "nums1 is spent" (`i < 0`) and "nums2's tail is $\ge$", so it is safe to test `nums1[i]` only after checking `i >= 0`. `p -= 1` always moves the write head left. Because $p$ is always *ahead* of both read pointers, no write ever clobbers a value not yet read — that is the whole reason back-fill needs no buffer, unlike the front version.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Merge into a copy** is $O((m+n)\log(m+n))$ time with the sort, $O(m+n)$ extra space. **Two-way merge into a fresh buffer** is $O(m+n)$ time — one comparison and one pointer move per output slot — but still $O(m+n)$ space. **Fill from the back** is $O(m+n)$ time and $O(1)$ space: the direction is the *only* thing that bought the space back. Note what made it possible: the spare room sits at the tail of the destination. Merge sort's merge step has no such spare room inside the array, which is why the textbook merge sort uses an $O(n)$ buffer.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 0$: `while j >= 0` never runs; $\mathit{nums1}$ untouched — correct.
- $m = 0$: only $\mathit{nums2}$ values are copied, from the back, into the all-zero buffer.
- Why stop at $j < 0$, not $i < 0$? Leftover $\mathit{nums1}[0 \dots i]$ are already in their final spots (they were never moved); leftover $\mathit{nums2}$ would *not* be, so $j$ is the one you must drain. Once $j < 0$, the write head equals $i$ ($p = i + j + 1 = i$), so continuing would only copy each $\mathit{nums1}[i]$ onto itself.
- Values reach $\pm 10^9$ — comparisons are fine, but keep any derived sums in `long long` (@sec-arr-cost).
:::

- [CF 600B · Queries about less or equal elements](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/600/B){rating="1300"} — sort both arrays and walk them together like a merge: for each query in sorted order, the count of $a_j \le b_i$ is where a forward finger in $a$ has stopped.
- [LC 21 · Merge Two Sorted Lists](https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-two-sorted-lists/){difficulty="Easy"} — the front merge with `next` pointers instead of indices.
- Then flip the direction of @sec-tp-p3-a on purpose (fill from the front, in place) and find the first input where a write clobbers an unread value.
:::
